title: Kingship, Government, and Justice
content: Royal succession, legitimacy, coronation, council politics, and limits on royal power.
Burhagohain, Borgohain, Borpatrogohain, Borbarua, Borphukan, and subordinate officers.
Provincial, local, frontier, household, and specialised departments and offices.
Judicial practice, petitions, customary rules, punishments, property disputes, and evidence gaps.
Appointments, service, gifts, royal orders, land grants, and institutional change over six centuries.
visual: A dated administration diagram and an office glossary.

title: The Paik System: Service, Land, and Obligation
content: Origins and successive reforms; distinguish early practices from later standardisation.
Paik categories, gots, khels, service rotation, officer hierarchy, and exemptions.
Links between land, cultivation, military duty, transport, construction, and craft labour.
Household burdens, displacement, desertion, unequal obligations, and dealings with religious institutions.
Breakdown, adaptation, and the system’s relationship to rebellion and colonial transition.
visual: A worked service-cycle example labelled with its historical period.

title: Army, Navy, Intelligence, and Fortifications
content: Recruitment, command, infantry, boats, horses, elephants, artillery, and changing weapons.
Shipbuilding, metalwork, gunpowder, workshops, procurement, and captured technology.
River warfare, earthworks, stockades, garhs, defensive systems, and campaigns on different terrain.
Scouting, information networks, diplomatic intelligence, logistics, disease, and supply.
Surrender, captives, booty, military labour, and the civilian costs of warfare.
visual: A military-system diagram, fort types, and annotated object photographs.

title: Land, Agriculture, and the Rural Economy
content: Wet rice, dry cultivation, irrigation, clearing, livestock, fisheries, and regional differences.
Land categories, service land, grants, transfers, obligations, and tenure disputes.
Village organisation, seasonal work, food storage, taxation, and state extraction.
Floods, erosion, famine, epidemic, war damage, and recovery where documented.
Change over time and the limits of reconstructing yields, incomes, or population from scattered sources.
visual: A seasonal calendar and dated land-category comparison.

title: Trade, Money, Markets, and Craft Production
content: Markets, river routes, roads, passes, frontier exchange, customs posts, and intermediaries.
Coins, mints, inscriptions, metal standards, barter, and changes in monetisation.
Silk, cotton, weaving, iron, brass, bell-metal, pottery, boats, arms, and other attested crafts.
Court workshops, specialist khels, merchants, imports, exports, and labour relations.
The economic effects of war, rebellion, early Company intervention, and shifting trading networks.
visual: A trade map, craft register, and coin plates with catalogue references.

title: Communities, Migration, and Social Hierarchy
content: Ahom identity and the kingdom’s diverse populations; avoid treating dynasty, language, and ethnicity as interchangeable.
Ahomisation, Assamese-language expansion, incorporation, intermarriage, and continuing distinct identities.
Caste, rank, clan, profession, noble households, service groups, slavery, and dependency.
Muslim communities, immigrants, captives, religious networks, and frontier mobility.
Present Ahom, Moran, Borahi, Chutiya, Dimasa, Koch, Mising, Matak, and other perspectives where source support exists.
visual: A community-and-institution matrix with changing historical names explained.

title: Women, Family, and Political Agency
content: Royal women, political marriages, succession, property, household authority, and court patronage.
Case studies of Mula Gabharu, Ramani Gabharu, Joymoti, Phuleswari, Ambika, Sarbeswari, and Kuranganayani.
Ordinary women’s cultivation, weaving, trade, ritual, household labour, and experiences of conflict.
Marriage, kinship, inheritance, sexuality, widowhood, captivity, and status as far as evidence permits.
Identify the limits imposed by male court authors and avoid presenting exceptional royal lives as universal experience.
visual: Comparative biographies and a table of evidence for ordinary women’s lives.

title: Religion, Ritual, and Religious Institutions
content: Tai-Ahom cosmology, ancestor traditions, ritual specialists, ceremonies, and changing royal practice.
Shaiva, Shakta, Vaishnava, and other religious traditions and their regional institutions.
Sankardeva, Madhavdeva, Ekasarana traditions, sattras, namghars, and their wider social influence.
Patronage, grants, labour exemptions, debate, conflict, and accommodation between court and religious authorities.
Date changes carefully and distinguish living traditions from practices demonstrated for a specific medieval century.
visual: A religious-institution map and a period-by-period patronage timeline.

title: Languages, Literature, Education, and Historical Memory
content: Tai-Ahom language and script, Assamese, Sanskrit, Persian contacts, and multilingual records.
Buranji production, scribes, archives, translation, circulation, and manuscript preservation.
Poetry, religious writing, drama, biography, technical texts, and court-sponsored learning.
Religious institutions, family instruction, literacy, libraries, and knowledge transmission.
Language change, genealogical memory, lost manuscripts, and later editing; distinguish original wording from modern translation.
visual: Manuscript facsimiles, script examples, and a genre-and-language register.

title: Capitals, Architecture, Roads, and Waterworks
content: Charaideo, Garhgaon, Rangpur, Jorhat, and temporary centres: dates, purposes, movement, and landscape.
Kareng Ghar, Talatal Ghar, Rang Ghar, temples, tanks, bridges, roads, forts, and provincial monuments.
Royal and religious patronage, design, materials, artisans, engineering, and labour.
Inscriptions, archaeological records, construction phases, damage, rebuilding, and mistaken attributions.
Evaluate famous claims about secret tunnels, construction recipes, and architectural influence with evidence.
visual: Capital plans and a monument gazetteer with source and dating fields.

title: Moidams, Objects, Art, and Royal Death
content: Funerary architecture, Charaideo and other sites, royal genealogy, burial and cremation practices.
Ritual, grave goods, cosmology, changing construction, and archaeology of funerary landscapes.
Coins, seals, weapons, regalia, sculpture, textiles, manuscripts, and museum objects.
What excavation can establish and what requires interpretation; source criticism for human-sacrifice claims.
Later damage, excavation, preservation, community custodianship, and a short clearly modern heritage note.
visual: Moidam sections, an object catalogue, and provenance labels.

title: Everyday Life, Environment, and Practical Knowledge
content: Housing, food, clothing, ornaments, markets, leisure, performance, festivals, and regional variation.
Agricultural calendars, astronomy, calendrical systems, medicine, veterinary knowledge, and technical manuscripts.
Floods, river shifts, forests, disease, animals, and environmental constraints.
The lives of cultivators, craftspeople, soldiers, servants, captives, children, and mobile communities.
Separate historical descriptions from modern customs and acknowledge topics for which evidence remains sparse.
visual: A source-based household reconstruction and seasonal-life diagram.

title: Why the Moamoria Rebellion Became Possible
content: Mayamora/Moamoria religious networks, social composition, and regional bases.
Labour obligations, elite power, patronage, inequalities, and religious tensions.
Court actions and reported incidents: compare sectarian and royal narratives.
The roles of caste, rank, ethnic affiliation, personal conflict, and regional politics.
An explicit comparison of competing explanations rather than assigning the rebellion one cause.
visual: A causes-and-evidence matrix and map of institutional networks.

title: Lakshmi Singha and the First Moamoria Uprising
content: Sunyeophaa/Lakshmi Singha: accession, ministers, household, and political vulnerability.
Rebellion leadership, mobilisation, capture of power, rival authority, and royal displacement.
Ramakanta, Raghav, Kuranganayani, and other actors with biographies tied to evidence.
Counter-mobilisation, restoration, punishment, and effects on labour and cultivation.
Chronology of suppression, renewed conflict, and the conditions inherited by Gaurinath.
visual: A rebellion-and-restoration timeline and actor chart.

title: Gaurinath Singha and Prolonged Civil War
content: Suhitpangphaa/Gaurinath Singha, noble factions, and the renewal and spread of conflict.
Rebel leaders, administrations, military fronts, and changes in control.
Royal flight, provincial disorder, loss of manpower, and disruption of revenue and farming.
Purnananda Burhagohain, the development of Jorhat, and political survival.
Distinguish phases and regional movements that compressed summaries often combine into one uprising.
visual: A year-by-year control map with disputed dates explicitly marked.

title: Captain Welsh and the First Company Intervention
content: Appeals for assistance and the Company’s political, military, and commercial interests.
Welsh’s expedition, route, operations, local alliances, and negotiations.
Military assistance, proposals for reform, supplies, payment, and correspondence.
British withdrawal and the limits of the intervention.
How contemporary participants and later historians interpreted its significance.
visual: An expedition map and a comparison of Assamese and Company correspondence.

title: Kamaleshwar Singha and Partial Reconstruction
content: Suklingphaa/Kamaleshwar Singha, court, household, and ministerial authority.
Purnananda’s administration, military recovery, settlement, and restoration of production.
Matak autonomy, leadership, settlements, and the politics of territorial compromise.
Continuing unrest, changing labour and military arrangements, and relations with neighbours.
The limits of recovery and the succession to Chandrakanta Singha.
visual: A reconstruction map and a post-rebellion settlement register.

title: Chandrakanta Singha and the Court’s Breakdown
content: Sudingphaa/Chandrakanta Singha: accession, household, factional politics, and competing officials.
Purnananda, Badan Chandra Borphukan, Ruchinath, and other principal actors.
Disputes over power, flight, appeals abroad, and the sequence leading to intervention.
Contacts with the Company, Burmese court, and other regional actors.
Distinguish documented decisions from later allegations of personal treachery or inevitability.
visual: A faction-and-diplomacy diagram and a dated pre-invasion sequence.

title: The First Burmese Intervention
content: Burmese/Konbaung interests and the political circumstances of the invitation.
Commanders, routes, battles, treaties or settlements, payments, and withdrawal.
Badan Chandra’s role and changes in court power.
Effects on the king, ministers, military organisation, inhabitants, and neighbouring polities.
Compare Assamese, Burmese, and Company records and reconcile different invasion counts.
visual: A first-intervention map and source-specific chronology.

title: Purandar Singha and the Second Intervention
content: Brajanath, Purandar Singha, Ruchinath, and the displacement of Chandrakanta.
Purandar’s accession, administration, opposition, and short first reign.
The renewed Burmese intervention, campaigns, flight, and Chandrakanta’s restoration.
Shifting alliances, attempts to regain authority, payments, and military resources.
Keep Purandar’s later 1833–1838 restoration in the contextual appendix rather than mixing the two reigns.
visual: A parallel succession-and-intervention timeline.

title: Chandrakanta’s Resistance and Jogeshwar Singha
content: Chandrakanta’s attempts to recover control, recruitment, allies, and recorded battles.
Jogeshwar Singha: lineage, installation, nominal status, household, and variant reign dates.
Burmese commanders and the actual distribution of power.
Flight, exile, rival royal claims, and the fragmentation of sovereignty.
Resolve differences in accounts of the final campaigns and the occupation’s end.
visual: A rival-claims timeline and a map of final resistance campaigns.

title: The Burmese Occupation and Civilian Catastrophe
content: Administration, extraction, garrisons, local collaborators, and changing forms of occupation.
Violence, captivity, flight, famine, depopulation, and loss of cultivation and settlements.
Experiences of women, children, religious institutions, and frontier communities.
The Manor Din memory tradition: compare contemporary reports with later oral and literary accounts.
Use ranges or qualitative descriptions where death tolls and population estimates cannot be established.
visual: A displacement map and a carefully sourced civilian-impact dossier.

title: The First Anglo-Burmese War and Yandabo
content: Company and Konbaung objectives and the war’s wider geography.
The Assam campaign, commanders, routes, battles, evacuation, and the end of Burmese control.
The Treaty of Yandabo: identify the signatories and analyse the Assam-related wording.
Distinguish Burma’s renunciation of claims from the subsequent means by which the Company governed Assam.
Responses of Ahom claimants, nobles, local communities, and neighbouring polities.
visual: A war map and an annotated treaty-clause comparison.

title: Company Rule and the Question of Restoration
content: David Scott and Company officials, territorial divisions, revenue, military control, and local intermediaries.
What proclamations and correspondence promised, and what decisions actually followed.
Royal claimants, displaced nobles, service holders, cultivators, and grievances.
Debates about restoring an Ahom ruler and the political status of Upper Assam.
Networks and circumstances that made a royal restoration movement possible.
visual: A colonial administration map and a promise-versus-policy document table.

title: Gomdhar Konwar: Biography, Claim, and Coronation
content: Name variants, family, royal descent, birthplace, upbringing, and evidence for each biographical claim.
Dhanjoy/Dhananjay Borgohain, Jairam/Jeuram Khargharia Phukan, and other supporters: verify identities and roles.
The assembly, coronation or installation, location, dates, rituals, and declared claim to authority.
Support networks, recruitment, resources, objectives, and relations with local communities.
Treat Gomdhar as a restoration claimant or rebel king as sources warrant; do not silently add him to the ordinary pre-occupation regnal sequence.
visual: A person-by-person evidence dossier and a coronation-site map.

title: The Uprising of 1828 and Gomdhar’s Fate
content: Plans, movement of supporters, attempted operations, Company intelligence, and suppression.
Neufville and other officials; arrest, surrender, proceedings, charges, and sentencing.
Conflicting accounts of punishment, commutation, imprisonment, exile, release, and later life; trace each to its earliest available record.
Why the movement failed, what it sought, and how historians interpret restoration and anti-colonial resistance.
Close the narrative on Gomdhar; place the separate 1830 uprising and 1833–1838 restoration in a short clearly out-of-period appendix.
visual: A day-by-day sequence where available and a final unresolved-questions register.
